Christian interpreters, such as Augustine, read the laugh as delight in God's justice rather than in a person's ruin. On prayers against enemies, see the topic on the curse psalms.

a: and grew strong in his ruinous schemes.
p: The Hebrew says he "was strong in his destruction." The Greek has "his vanity"; others read "his wealth."
b: Ya'oz behavvato is "he grew strong in his destruction" (the ruin he caused others, the word of 52:2, "ruin"). The Greek has "in his vanity" (en tē mataiotēti autou). The Syriac and Targum are often cited as reading behono, "in his wealth," which matches the line before. The sense in every case is that he relied on his own power and money instead of making God his stronghold (ma'oz), with a play on ya'oz, "he was strong."

a: But I am a leafy olive tree in God's house;
t: An olive tree in the temple court
p: The olive lives for centuries and stays green. Trees may really have grown in the temple courts.
b: The olive tree is evergreen and can live for hundreds of years; it was a picture of a blessed and lasting life (128:3; Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). Trees may have grown in the temple courts (92:13, "Planted in the LORD's house"; Zechariah 4 has two olive trees by the lampstand). The contrast with 52:5 is complete: the liar is uprooted from his tent, the trusting one is rooted in God's house. "Loyal love" answers 52:1.

a: On mahalath.
p: An unknown musical term, also in the title of Psalm 88. It may mean a sad tune or a kind of flute.
b: Al machalat appears only here and in 88:0 ("on mahalath leannoth"). Proposals: a tune name; from chalah, "be sick," a mournful melody; from chalil, "flute"; or a dance (mecholah). The Greek simply transliterated it (hyper maeleth). The rest of the title, "a maskil of David," differs from Psalm 14's "Of David," one of several small changes between the two copies.

a: the fool says to himself.
t: The fool: not an atheist in the modern sense
p: A nabal is morally foolish, a person who lives as if God will never act, not someone with a theory.
b: Naval is the fool who acts shamefully, without regard for God or neighbor, like Nabal, whose name means "fool" (1 Samuel 25:25: "As his name is, so is he"). "There is no God" (en elohim) in the ancient world did not usually deny that a god existed. It meant: God is not here, he does not see or care, he will not judge (10:4, 11; 94:7). This is practical atheism, the life lived as if there were no judge. It is the same "fool" Jesus describes in Luke 12:20. The psalm says nothing about the intelligence of people who doubt God; its target is moral corruption: "They have gone rotten... Not one of them does good."
orig: אָמַר נָבָל בְּלִבּוֹ אֵין אֱלֹהִים ('amar naval belibbo en elohim)

a: They have gone rotten, and their injustice is detestable.
p: Psalm 14:1 has 'alilah, "deeds"; Psalm 53:1 has 'avel, "injustice," and adds "and."
b: Psalm 14:1 reads hishchitu hit'ivu 'alilah, "they are corrupt, they do abhorrent deeds." Psalm 53:1 reads hishchitu vehit'ivu 'avel, "they are corrupt and do abhorrent injustice." The words 'alilah and 'avel look alike in Hebrew letters, and either could come from the other by a scribe's slip or a deliberate sharpening. "Corrupt" (shachat) is the verb of Genesis 6:11–12, where "the earth was corrupt" before the flood. "Detestable" is ta'av, the root of to'evah, rendered "abhorrent" elsewhere on this site. The Plain English Translation of 53:1–4 and 53:6 matches the site's Psalm 14 wherever the Hebrew is the same. See the chapter page for every difference between the two psalms.

a: From heaven God leans out and looks at the human race,
t: God looks down, as before the flood and Babel
p: God looking down on humanity recalls Genesis 6 and 11. Psalm 14:2 has "the LORD" here.
b: The picture of God looking down from heaven (hishqif) to inspect humans recalls Genesis 6:5–12 (God sees that the earth is corrupt) and Genesis 11:5 (he comes down to see the tower). Here Psalm 14:2 reads "the LORD," and 53:2 "God." "Any act wisely" (maskil) uses the same word as the psalm's title: the one who acts wisely is the one who seeks God (doresh et-elohim). Paul strings 53:1–3 (or 14:1–3) with other verses in Romans 3:10–12 to show that "Jews and Greeks alike: all of them are under sin" (Romans 3:9).

a: Every one has slid back; all alike have turned sour.
p: Ne'elachu means "gone sour, rotten," used of spoiled food. Psalm 14:3 has a different verb for "turned."
b: Psalm 14:3 reads hakkol sar, "all have strayed, turned aside"; Psalm 53:3 reads kullo sag, "all of it has backed away, slid back" (the verb sug, as in 44:18, "our hearts did not slip backward"). The second verb, ne'elachu, is used in Job 15:16 of a person "vile and corrupt" and in Arabic of milk going sour. Romans 3:12 quotes the Greek: "All have turned away; together they have become useless."
orig: כֻּלּוֹ סָג יַחְדָּו נֶאֱלָחוּ (kullo sag yachdav ne'elachu)

a: They devour my people as they would eat bread,
p: The powerful consume the poor as casually as a meal, as Micah 3:2–3 says of Jerusalem's leaders.
b: Those who "eat" God's people are not foreign invaders but powerful insiders who exploit the poor as easily and as daily as they eat bread. Micah 3:2–3 accuses Jerusalem's rulers of tearing the skin off the people and eating their flesh; Proverbs 30:14 speaks of those whose teeth are swords "to devour the poor." "My people" may be God speaking, or the psalmist speaking for the oppressed. They do not call on God: their practical atheism (53:1) shows in both injustice and prayerlessness.

a: There they shook with dread,
p: Here the two psalms part ways. Psalm 53 has a battle scene; Psalm 14 speaks of God with the righteous.
b: Psalm 14:5–6 reads (literally): "There they dreaded a dread, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plan of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge." Psalm 53:5 reads, also literally: "There they dreaded a dread, where (or such as) there was no dread, for God has scattered the bones of your besieger; you have put them to shame, for God has rejected them." Several Hebrew words are similar in shape and sound, so many scholars think one text was rewritten, or misread, from the other. In Psalm 53 the scene has become a military rout: an army camped against Zion is struck and its bones lie unburied, a terrible disgrace (Jeremiah 8:1–2; Ezekiel 6:5). Some link it with Sennacherib's army (2 Kings 19:35). "There was no dread" may mean they panicked with no cause, or felt a terror like nothing before.
r: Psalm 14:5–6; Jeremiah 8:1–2; Ezekiel 6:5; 2 Kings 19:35; Leviticus 26:17; Proverbs 28:1

a: When God brings his people back from captivity,
p: Shuv shevut can mean bringing back captives or, more broadly, turning a people's fortunes around.
b: Shuv shevut is an idiom with a sound play: "turn the turning." It was long read as "bring back the captivity" (KJV), which suggests the exile. In Job 42:10 God "restored the fortunes" of Job, who was never a captive, so many now render it "restore the fortunes" in general. If the exile is meant, the closing verse would be an addition from that period; if not, it is a general prayer for Israel's renewal. The wish formula "who will give..." (mi yitten) is the Hebrew way of saying "if only." Psalm 53:6 has "rescues" (plural, yeshu'ot) where Psalm 14:7 has the singular, and "God" for "the LORD"; the Plain English Translation gives "saving help" for the plural, as in 42:5, and so differs from Psalm 14 here.
orig: בְּשׁוּב אֱלֹהִים שְׁבוּת עַמּוֹ (beshuv elohim shevut 'ammo)

a: when the Ziphites came and said to Saul,
p: Twice the people of Ziph, a town in Judah, told Saul where David was hiding.
b: Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, south-east of Hebron. "Men of Ziph went up to Saul at Gibeah. 'Did you know David is hiding out near us?' they said" (1 Samuel 23:19). They did so again in 1 Samuel 26:1. The title quotes the question almost exactly. The betrayal was by David's own tribe, which suits the psalm's "outsiders" only if the word means people who acted like strangers (see 54:3). The second time, David spared Saul's life in his camp (1 Samuel 26).

a: By your name, O God, rescue me;
p: God's name is God himself as he has made himself known. It is the power the speaker appeals to.
b: In Hebrew thought a name is the person as known and called on. "Your name" stands parallel with "your power" (gevurah). To be saved by God's name is to be saved by God himself, the one who revealed his name to Moses (Exodus 3:13–15) and put it in the temple (1 Kings 8:29). Proverbs 18:10 calls the LORD's name "a strong tower." The psalm ends with thanks to the same name (54:6), which makes a frame around the prayer. "Win my case" (din) uses a law-court verb: "judge in my favor."

a: For outsiders have stood up against me,
p: Zarim means strangers or outsiders. Psalm 86:14, nearly the same line, has zedim, "the arrogant."
b: The Masoretic Text has zarim, "strangers, outsiders," and the Greek agrees (allotrioi). Psalm 86:14 repeats this verse almost word for word but with zedim, "arrogant men," and the Targum and some Hebrew manuscripts are reported to read zedim here too. The two words differ by one letter (r and d look alike in Hebrew script). The Ziphites of the title were fellow Judeans, so "outsiders" would mean people who acted like strangers. "Give God no place before their eyes" means they do not reckon with God at all (compare 36:1; Romans 3:18).

a: the Lord is among those who hold up my life.
p: The Hebrew "in those who sustain" probably means "the Lord is the one who sustains," a common idiom.
b: Literally "the Lord is among those who sustain my life." This could imply that God is one helper among others, but Hebrew often uses "in" (be-) to mean "as, in the role of" (grammarians call it the beth of essence), as in Exodus 18:4, where "The God of my father came to help me" is literally "the God of my father was in my help." So most read: "the Lord is the upholder of my life." The Plain English Translation keeps the literal form. Note "the Lord" here is Adonai, not YHWH.

a: He will turn the evil back on those who spy on me.
t: Written "let it return", read "he will return"
p: The written text (Ketiv) has "the evil will return"; the reading tradition (Qere) has "he will return the evil."
b: The consonants (Ketiv) read yashuv hara', "the evil will turn back (on them)": evil boomerangs on its makers, as in 7:15–16. The reading tradition (Qere) is yashiv, "he will turn back the evil," making God the one who acts. The Greek has "he will turn back" (apostrepsei). The Plain English Translation follows the Qere with the Greek. "Those who spy on me" (shorerai) are those who watch for a chance to attack (also 5:8; 27:11). "Put an end to them" (hatsmitem) means destroy, not merely silence.

a: I will offer you a sacrifice of my own free will;
p: A nedavah was an offering given out of gratitude, not because the law required it.
b: Nedavah is the freewill offering, a peace offering brought willingly (Leviticus 7:16; 22:18–23; Numbers 15:3). The speaker vows to bring one when God rescues him. This is the first time the name YHWH appears in the psalm: "I will thank your name, LORD." In the Elohistic Psalter such a lone use of the name stands out (compare 42:8 and 55:16).

a: and my eye has gazed on my enemies.
p: The Hebrew says only that his eye "has looked on" his enemies. "In triumph" or "its desire" is added in English.
b: The idiom ra'ah be-, "look on," often carries the sense of seeing an enemy's downfall with satisfaction (59:10; 92:11; 112:8; 118:7), and many versions add "in triumph" or, like the KJV, "his desire." The Hebrew itself is short: "my eye has looked on my enemies." The past tense may be the prophetic perfect, speaking of a rescue that is certain, or a thanksgiving added after the rescue came.

a: A maskil of David.
p: The title names no event. Tradition linked the false friend with Ahithophel, and the church with Judas.
b: Psalm 55 is a lament over a city full of violence and a close friend turned enemy (55:12–14, 20–21). The title names no occasion. Jewish and Christian interpreters have often connected it with Absalom's revolt, when David's trusted counselor Ahithophel joined the plot (2 Samuel 15:12, 31) and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). The Talmud notes that Doeg and Ahithophel both died young, fulfilling 55:23 (Bavli Sanhedrin 106b). Christian writers from Augustine on heard in the friend's betrayal the voice of Christ betrayed by Judas (compare John 13:18, which quotes Psalm 41:9). Many scholars think instead of an unnamed leader in a troubled Jerusalem, perhaps late in the monarchy.

a: I wander restless in my complaint, and I groan
p: Arid is a rare verb meaning to roam or be restless. Siach, "complaint," is anxious, spoken-out thought.
b: Arid comes from rud, "to roam, wander restlessly" (Jeremiah 2:31; Genesis 27:40). The speaker cannot settle. Siach means musing, talking to oneself, pouring out a complaint (102:0; 142:2; Hannah's word in 1 Samuel 1:16). "Groan" (hum, or hamah) is a low moaning sound, like the groaning in 42:5. The verbs of 55:2–5 pile up the body's response to fear: restless, groaning, writhing, trembling, shuddering.

a: And I said, "Who will give me wings like a dove's?
t: "O for the wings of a dove"
p: The wish to escape is one of the most quoted lines in the Psalter, and a well-loved song by Mendelssohn.
b: "Who will give me" (mi yitten li) is the Hebrew "if only." The rock dove nests in the cliffs and ravines of the wilderness (Jeremiah 48:28; Song of Songs 2:14), far from the city's violence (55:9–11). The speaker longs not to fight but to flee, and the poem admits that longing honestly before it turns to trust (55:16, 22). Felix Mendelssohn's anthem "Hear my prayer" (1844), with its solo "O for the wings of a dove," is a setting of a paraphrase of 55:1–7. Jeremiah 9:2 voices the same wish for a lodging in the wilderness.

a: Confuse them, Lord, split their speech,
p: "Split their tongue" recalls the tower of Babel, where God mixed up language and stopped a city's plans.
b: Ballaʿ is "swallow" or "confuse," and pallag leshonam is "divide their tongue." The pairing recalls Genesis 11:7, "let us go down and mix up their language there," and the name Peleg, in whose days the earth "was split up" (Genesis 10:25, from the same root palag). The city of violence is to suffer Babel's fate: its leaders no longer able to agree on their plots. The Greek has "drown, Lord, and divide their tongues" (katapontison).
orig: בַּלַּע אֲדֹנָי פַּלַּג לְשׁוֹנָם (balla' adonai pallag leshonam)

a: They make their rounds of it on its walls by day and night,
p: Violence and strife are pictured as sentries walking the city walls, the job of the city's guards.
b: Normally watchmen walk the walls to protect a city (127:1; Song of Songs 5:7; Isaiah 62:6). Here "violence and strife" (55:9) are the ones making the rounds, and inside the city "evil and misery," "destruction," "harm and deceit" have settled in the public square, the open place by the gate where courts met and business was done (Ruth 4:1). The city meant to be a refuge (48:3) has become the danger. Jeremiah 6:6–7 and Ezekiel 22 bring the same charges against Jerusalem.

a: But it was you, a man of my own rank,
p: The poem suddenly speaks to the traitor: an equal, a close friend who worshiped beside him.
b: Enosh ke'erki, "a man of my value," is a man of equal rank. Alluf is a close friend or companion (Proverbs 16:28: "a gossip splits up the closest of friends"), and meyudda', "one known," an intimate. They "made sweet" their secret talks (sod, private counsel) and walked to the temple together in the festival crowd (regesh). That is why the betrayal hurts more than an enemy's attack. Jesus' word to Judas, "Friend, get on with what you came for" (Matthew 26:50), and the Gospel's "one who ate my bread" (John 13:18, from Psalm 41:9) recall the same grief.
orig: אֱנוֹשׁ כְּעֶרְכִּי אַלּוּפִי וּמְיֻדָּעִי (enosh ke'erki allufi umeyudda'i)

a: Let death come on them by surprise;
p: The written text has yeshimavet, "desolation"; the reading tradition splits it: "let death come by surprise."
b: The consonants (Ketiv) read as one word, yeshimavet, "desolation" (compare the place Beth-jeshimoth, Numbers 33:49): "Desolation on them!" The reading tradition (Qere) divides it into two words, yashshi mavet, "let death deceive (catch by surprise)" them. The Greek has "let death come on them." The Plain English Translation follows the Qere. "Let them go down to Sheol alive" recalls Korah and his men, who "went down alive to Sheol" (Numbers 16:33), which is striking in a book where Korah's sons are singers (42:0).
orig: יַשִּׁי מָוֶת (Qere yashshi mavet) / ישימות (Ketiv yeshimavet)

a: let them go down to Sheol alive,
p: The speaker asks God to kill his betrayers. How have Jews and Christians prayed such words?
b: The plea that the traitors die and go down to Sheol is one of the Psalter's curses, though briefer than Psalms 35, 69, 109 and 137. Readers have handled it in several ways: as an honest cry of the wronged that hands vengeance over to God instead of taking it (Romans 12:19; Deuteronomy 32:35); as a prayer against evil itself, which the church can pray against sin and the devil (Augustine, Cassiodorus); or as words that Christians, after Jesus' command to love enemies, should pray only with care or not at all (Matthew 5:44; Luke 23:34). The Roman Liturgy of the Hours (1971) leaves the harshest curse verses out of a number of psalms (General Instruction 131). See the topic on the curse psalms.

a: At evening, at morning, at midday
p: The rabbis read this verse, with Daniel's practice, as a source for Judaism's three daily prayers.
b: The order "evening, morning, midday" follows the Hebrew day, which begins at sunset. Daniel prays three times a day facing Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). The Talmud connects the three daily prayers of Judaism (evening Arvit, morning Shacharit, afternoon Minchah) with the patriarchs and with the temple's daily offerings (Bavli Berakhot 26b), and cites this verse and Daniel for praying three times a day (Bavli Berakhot 31a). The early church kept set hours of prayer too (Acts 3:1; 10:9; Didache 8:3, "pray this way three times a day"), which grew into the daily office.

a: though many stood against me.
p: The Hebrew "many were with me" probably means "against me" here. Some read it of angels on his side.
b: Ki verabbim hayu 'immadi is literally "for in (as) many they were with me." In context of a battle, "with" means "against" (as in English "fight with"), so most read: many fought against me. Some older interpreters read it as "many were on my side," either human allies or God's unseen army, as when Elisha says, "There are more with us than with them" (2 Kings 6:16). The Greek has "for among many they were with me." The verse as a whole is in the past: God "has bought back" the speaker's life, perhaps an answer already received.

a: For them there is no change of heart,
p: Chalifot means changes. It may mean they never reform, or never suffer reversal, or keep no agreements.
b: Asher en chalifot lamo, "for whom there are no changes." Readings: (1) they never change their ways, they do not repent; (2) life has never turned against them, so they feel no need of God (compare Jeremiah 48:11, Moab "settled on its dregs," never poured from jar to jar); (3) from a related word for an exchange or oath, they keep no agreements, which fits 55:20. "Humble them" in the first line reads ya'anem as "answer them" in the sense "afflict, humble" (the Greek tapeinōsei). The Hebrew of 55:18–21 is difficult throughout.
orig: אֲשֶׁר אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ ('asher en chalifot lamo)

a: The butter-talk of his mouth was smooth,
p: The Hebrew is literally "smooth were the butters of his mouth": flattering words that hide a sword.
b: Machma'ot, from chem'ah, "butter, curds," gives the image of creamy, soft words. Many scholars divide the letters differently to read mechem'ah panav, "his face was smoother than butter," and the Greek read something like "they were divided by the anger of his face," from chemah, "anger." The contrast is clear in every reading: smooth outside, war inside. Proverbs 5:3–4 uses the same pair, oil and sword, of flattering speech, and Proverbs 26:24–26 warns of the enemy who disguises himself with his lips.

a: Throw your load on the LORD,
t: 1 Peter 5:7: cast your care on him
p: Yehav, "what is given you to carry," is a rare word. The Greek "care, worry" is behind 1 Peter 5:7.
b: Yehavkha occurs only here. It is usually derived from yahav, "to give," so "what has been given to you, your lot, your burden." The Talmud reports that an Arab merchant used the word to mean "your load" (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 26b). The Greek translated it as "your care, anxiety" (tēn merimnan sou), and 1 Peter 5:7 echoes the Greek: "throwing all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you." The promise "he will provide for you" (yekhalkelekha) uses the verb for supplying food, as Joseph fed his family (Genesis 45:11). The speaker here turns to teach others what he has learned.

a: will not reach half their days.
p: The Talmud says Doeg died at 34 and Ahithophel at 33, not reaching half of seventy years.
b: A full life was seventy or eighty years (90:10). "Men of blood and deceit" will die before reaching half of it. The rabbis applied the verse to the two traitors of David's life: Doeg (Psalm 52) and Ahithophel (traditionally Psalm 55) did not live half their days (Bavli Sanhedrin 106b). "The well of the Pit" doubles two words for the grave. The psalm ends, after all its turmoil, on three words in Hebrew: "and I, I trust in you."
